title: Best Electric Heaters UK
short: Oil-filled, convector, infrared and fan heaters compared by type, running cost and who they suit.
intro: Electric heaters differ hugely in how they heat and what they cost to run. This guide compares the types and the models Mumsnet's panel picked, with their estimated running costs, so you can choose between whole-room warmth and heating just yourself. Safety guidance below comes from Electrical Safety First, a UK charity, not from the product reviews.

products.name: Dragon 4 TRDX41025E
products.best_for: Heating a room steadily over long periods
products.summary: An oil-filled radiator with three heat settings, a thermostat and a timer. Mumsnet says it gives steady heat and keeps warming after switch-off.
products.search: De'Longhi Dragon 4 TRDX41025E oil filled radiator

products.name: Convector Heater 2kW
products.summary: A very cheap, silent and lightweight convector with three heat settings and an adjustable thermostat, though it heats slowly and has no timer.

products.name: Curved Panel Infrared Heater
products.best_for: Personal warmth at a desk or beside furniture
products.summary: A low-power infrared panel that warms people and objects directly rather than the whole room. It is silent and light but has a hot front panel and no tip-over cut-out, per Mumsnet.
cons: Heats objects and people, not whole rooms

products.name: Oscillating Halogen Heater
products.summary: A halogen heater with three settings and oscillation that gives instant warmth, and a tip-over shut-off. Mumsnet notes a short cable and flimsy construction.

products.name: Hot+Cool HF1
products.best_for: Buyers who want heating and cooling in one, with app control
products.summary: A premium fan that heats in winter and cools in summer, with Wi-Fi app scheduling and a remote. It is very expensive.

products.name: Silent Power Eco Fan Heater
products.best_for: Powerful room heating with an eco mode
products.summary: A compact fan heater with four modes, a 1-9 hour timer and an eco setting, with a humid-room rating. Mumsnet notes it has not been independently tested.
products.search: Dreamland Silent Power Eco fan heater

products.name: 2500873 11 Fin Digital
products.best_for: Larger spaces on a budget, with app-free digital control
products.summary: Expert Reviews found this reached 20°C in 30 minutes and held a consistent temperature, with a digital thermostat and remote-controlled 24-hour timer at a budget price.

specs.Extras: Digital thermostat, 24-hour timer with remote, Eco mode

pros: Rapid heating (20°C in 30 minutes in testing)
products.search: VonHaus 2500873 11 Fin Digital oil filled radiator

products.name: RH0FR3001
products.best_for: Small rooms and compact spaces where portability matters
products.summary: A lightweight, low-power oil-filled radiator with a carrying handle, well suited to a small room, though Expert Reviews found it struggles in larger spaces.

specs.Extras: Single thermostat dial, overheat protection, carrying handle

guide.q: Which type of electric heater is cheapest to run?
guide.a: All electric heaters turn nearly all the electricity they use into heat, so running cost depends on wattage and how long you run them. Low-power infrared panels are cheapest for heating one person. For a whole room, a thermostat helps avoid heating for longer than needed.
Oil-filled radiators heat slowly but steadily and keep giving off heat after switch-off. Convectors give background warmth. Fan heaters heat a room fastest but can be noisy.

guide.q: What safety features should I look for?
guide.a: Electrical Safety First recommends a heater with a tip-over cut-off and, for halogen heaters especially, a cool-to-touch surface. Keep vents clear of dust so the heater does not overheat, and buy from a reputable retailer rather than secondhand.

guide.q: Is it safe to leave an electric heater on overnight?
guide.a: Electrical Safety First advises against running any heater unattended or overnight. If you do need overnight background heat, an oil-filled radiator is a lower-risk choice than a fan or halogen heater, but check the manufacturer's own instructions first.

guide.q: Where should I place a heater, and can I use an extension lead?
guide.a: Keep it at least a metre from curtains, furniture and paper, on a level surface out of the way of foot traffic. Electrical Safety First advises plugging heaters directly into a wall socket rather than an extension lead, which can overload and become a fire risk. Never dry clothes on or near a heater, and make sure you have working smoke alarms.
